cards.front: What is an air mass?
back: A large body of air with similar temperature and moisture.

cards.front: Which air mass usually brings mild, wet weather from the Atlantic?
back: Tropical maritime.

cards.front: What is continentality?
back: The effect of distance from the sea on climate.

cards.front: Give one renewable energy source.
back: Wind power.

cards.front: What gas makes biogas useful as a fuel?
back: Methane.

cards.front: Name the UK flood case study used in this course.
back: Somerset Levels.

cards.front: Explain how the North Atlantic Drift affects the UK climate.
back: It transfers warm ocean water towards north-west Europe.
This helps make UK winters milder than places at a similar latitude.

cards.front: Explain why western uplands are generally wetter than eastern lowlands.
back: Moist Atlantic air is forced to rise over upland relief.
It cools, condenses and produces rainfall before descending towards the east.

cards.front: Give two effects of flooding on people.
back: Homes or businesses may be damaged.
Roads may be cut off, disrupting travel and services.

cards.front: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of a reservoir.
back: Advantage: it stores water for periods of high demand or low rainfall.
Disadvantage: it floods land and can damage habitats or communities.

cards.front: Explain why wind power needs support from storage or other energy sources.
back: Wind speed varies, so output is intermittent.
Supply must still meet demand when turbines generate little electricity.

cards.front: Give two products of anaerobic digestion.
back: Biogas.
Digestate.

cards.front: Explain how prolonged rainfall can cause river flooding.
back: Rain fills soil stores until the ground becomes saturated.
More water then flows over the surface or rapidly through the soil into rivers.
Discharge rises above channel capacity and water spills onto the floodplain.

cards.front: Explain why the Somerset Levels are vulnerable to flooding.
back: The landscape is very low and flat; about 18% of Somerset lies below average high-tide level.
Water drains slowly through rivers and artificial channels, especially when the ground is saturated.
High tides can restrict river outflow, so water spreads widely across the Levels.

cards.front: Explain one environmental problem caused by intensive food production.
back: Large fertiliser inputs can be washed into rivers.
Nutrients encourage excessive algal growth.
Decomposition then reduces oxygen, harming aquatic life.

cards.front: Explain how anaerobic digestion produces useful energy.
back: Microorganisms break down organic material in a sealed tank without oxygen.
This releases methane-rich biogas.
The gas is burned in suitable equipment to produce heat or electricity.

cards.front: Explain how air masses and continentality create contrasting UK weather.
back: Tropical maritime air crosses the Atlantic and brings mild, moist conditions.
Polar continental air can bring cold, dry conditions from eastern Europe.
Coastal places are moderated by the sea because water heats and cools slowly.
Inland areas have a greater temperature range because land changes temperature faster.

cards.front: Explain how two long-term strategies reduce flood risk on the Somerset Levels.
back: Dredging selected sections of the Parrett and Tone increases channel capacity; programmes in 2014, 2016 and 2018 removed about 270,500 m³ of silt.
Raising the Muchelney–Drayton road maintains community access during floods, reducing isolation even when surrounding land stores water.

cards.front: Explain why the UK's energy mix has changed since 1950.
back: Domestic coal declined as mines closed and pollution and carbon concerns grew.
Oil and gas became important for transport, heating and electricity.
Nuclear provided dependable low-operational-carbon electricity.
Falling costs, technology and climate policy encouraged growth in renewables.

cards.front: Explain two disadvantages of Hinkley Point C.
back: A very large, lengthy construction project creates traffic, accommodation pressure, cost and local habitat or landscape disturbance.
Radioactive waste from electricity generation must be securely managed for far longer than the station's planned 60-year operating life.
